newsitem.title: USA: Miami report - Fuel surcharge edges Latam rates up.
newsitem.headline: Miami report - Fuel surcharge edges Latam rates up.

text.p: Cargo carriers that serve Latin America are beginning to slap fuel surcharges on some routes just as carriers and freight forwarders head into the busy season, a Reuter survey showed.

Several carriers, including Fine Airlines Inc and the TACA group from El Salvador, have added a five cents per kilo fuel surcharge as of Oct one and some airlines have warned the surcharge may go to seven cents by the end of the month, forwarders said.
"From the looks of it, everyone will follow this time," said one forwarder."
"They are doing it because they can. This is the busy season," said another forwarder.
The surcharges coincide with Miami International Airport's busiest season. Novermber is traditionally the heaviest month for cargo at MIA and all those polled expect a strong quarter this year.
"The fourth quarter is starting pretty strong. It is exciting," said one forwarder.

Northbound cargo coming from Latin America "is stronger than last year," said one airline executive. Generally airlines have trouble filling the northbound flights from many Latin American destinations.
In fact, forwarders grumbled that because the fourth quarter is so busy at MIA, carriers begin to push rates up by creating different tiers of rates or adding special charges.
The fuel surcharge is not reflected in the chart, because it is not yet widespread. So, for example, the Bogota rate of 60 cents is unchanged from the prior survey.
However, several major carriers are charging the fuel surcharge on that route, so that rate is likely to go up over the next few weeks as the surcharge becomes more widespread, forwarders said.
"All that comes to an end in January when things slow down," said one forwarder.

Shippers face a double bind in the fourth quarter. Freight volumes are heaviest during these months, and passenger carriers, which carry a lot of freight out of MIA to Latin America, are all but out of the market, airlines said.
"Our passenger loads are very, very heavy," said an executive at one big MIA passenger carrier, "we just don't have the capacity on our aircraft."
Beginning Nov 15 "we slow down the flow of cargo on almost every route," he added.

Passenger carriers do not have to restrict the cargo northbound from Latin America because passenger traffic and luggage is lighter from most points. Shippers can also select from abundant freighter lift on the less packed northbound routes.

Traffic to Brazil is very strong, said one forwarder. "We've seen an increase in service to Brazil. Polar Air Cargo had three full flights last weekend," he said, "and they were big birds," referring to the Boeing 747s Polar flies.
Despite the busy Brazil traffic, rates are unchanged at about $1.90 per kilo.
Looking east, rates to London from Miami still hover around $1.00 per kilo, but executives are looking for that to increase as the busy holiday charter season subsides.
"Give us another month," said one executive for a European carrier, and rates will firm to a more normal level.

"All these charter companies use GSAs to sell the belly capacity at very cheap rates," complained another European airline executive, "the charter airlines do not necessarily give the same kind of service, but it affects the rates."

So far, the charters have affected mostly European routes, but this executive predicted Latin America will fall into the same pattern as those countries continue to develop and spend more on vacations.

"It is only a matter of time before South American (holiday passenger) charters will go directly to Orlando (location of Disney World and other attractions) and put pressure on Latin American rates," he said.

A flurry of activity soon will begin from the Caribbean as Haiti's two month-long mango season starts about Nov. 1. Although some mangos are ocean shipped, many come by air. - Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 7706 Fax+44 171 542 5017
